claim: The lateral cerebellum is a neurobiological system that is novel to mammals.
source: We investigate the lateral cerebellum, a neurobiological system that is novel to mammals, and is associated with higher cognitive functions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of the lateral cerebellum.

claim: The lateral cerebellum is associated with higher cognitive functions.
source: We investigate the lateral cerebellum, a neurobiological system that is novel to mammals, and is associated with higher cognitive functions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of the lateral cerebellum.

claim: Relative volumetric changes of the lateral cerebellar hemispheres (independent of cerebellar size) are correlated with measures of domain-general cognition in primates.
source: We map the evolutionary diversification of the mammalian cerebellum and find that relative volumetric changes of the lateral cerebellar hemispheres (independent of cerebellar size) are correlated with measures of domain-general cognition in primates
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic regression analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: Lateral cerebellar hemisphere expansion is characterized by a combination of parallel and convergent shifts towards similar levels of expansion in distantly related mammalian lineages.
source: We map the evolutionary diversification of the mammalian cerebellum and find that relative volumetric changes of the lateral cerebellar hemispheres (independent of cerebellar size) are correlated with measures of domain-general cognition in primates, and are characterized by a combination of parallel and convergent shifts towards similar levels of expansion in distantly related mammalian lineages.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by evolutionary modeling in the Results section.

claim: Multiple independent evolutionary occurrences of increased behavioral complexity in mammals may at least partly be explained by selection on the cerebellum.
source: Results suggest that multiple independent evolutionary occurrences of increased behavioral complexity in mammals may at least partly be explained by selection on a common neural system, the cerebellum
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results stated in the abstract.

claim: The cerebellum may have been subject to multiple independent neurodevelopmental remodeling events during mammalian evolution.
source: Results suggest that multiple independent evolutionary occurrences of increased behavioral complexity in mammals may at least partly be explained by selection on a common neural system, the cerebellum, which may have been subject to multiple independent neurodevelopmental remodeling events during mammalian evolution.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results stated in the abstract.

claim: Tool manipulation is an adaptive behavior related to higher-order cognitive capacities.
source: Changes in neurobiological features that directly relate to higher-order cognitive capacities are particularly relevant as they underpin adaptive behaviors such as tool manipulation (Krützen et al., 2005; Boesch and Boesch, 1990)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Flexible problem solving is an adaptive behavior related to higher-order cognitive capacities.
source: Changes in neurobiological features that directly relate to higher-order cognitive capacities are particularly relevant as they underpin adaptive behaviors such as tool manipulation (Krützen et al., 2005; Boesch and Boesch, 1990), flexible problem solving (Benson-Amram et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Planning for the future is an adaptive behavior related to higher-order cognitive capacities.
source: Changes in neurobiological features that directly relate to higher-order cognitive capacities are particularly relevant as they underpin adaptive behaviors such as tool manipulation (Krützen et al., 2005; Boesch and Boesch, 1990), flexible problem solving (Benson-Amram et al., 2016), planning for the future (Raby et al., 2007; Osvath and Osvath, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sophisticated communication systems are adaptive behaviors related to higher-order cognitive capacities.
source: Changes in neurobiological features that directly relate to higher-order cognitive capacities are particularly relevant as they underpin adaptive behaviors such as tool manipulation (Krützen et al., 2005; Boesch and Boesch, 1990), flexible problem solving (Benson-Amram et al., 2016), planning for the future (Raby et al., 2007; Osvath and Osvath, 2008), and sophisticated communication systems (Janik, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Instances of intelligent behavior have evolved independently in different lineages of mammals.
source: Even though it is commonly agreed that instances of intelligent behavior have evolved independently in different lineages of mammals (Roth and Dicke, 2005; Roth, 2015)
evidence: This is stated as commonly agreed upon and supported by citations.

claim: It is unclear whether convergent behavioral abilities arose from modifications of common neural systems or whether lineage-specific contingency has shaped particular brain circuits according to unique socioecological conditions.
source: it is unclear whether such convergent behavioral abilities arose from modifications of common neural systems or whether lineage-specific contingency has shaped particular brain circuits according to unique socioecological conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the field.

claim: General intelligence has been proposed to equip species with the ability to make mental models of the environment, develop actions based on abstract notions of associations between percepts, and to generate goals from current contexts.
source: Such 'general intelligence' has been proposed to equip species with the ability to make mental models of the environment, develop actions based on abstract notions of associations between percepts, and to generate goals from current contexts (Spearman, 1904; Duncan et al., 2000; Genovesio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intelligence comprises the aggregate of cognitive modules of special abilities that evolved within a species in response to specific environments.
source: A different view holds that intelligence comprises the aggregate of cognitive modules of special abilities that evolved within a species in response to specific environments (Barkow et al., 1995; Cosmides and Tooby, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The cerebellum's structural, connectional, functional, and developmental anatomy is relatively uniform.
source: First, unlike the more commonly investigated cerebral cortex, the cerebellum's structural, connectional, functional, and developmental anatomy is relatively uniform (Larsell, 1970)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The cerebellum is ideal for the comparison of homologous neural circuits across species.
source: the cerebellum's structural, connectional, functional, and developmental anatomy is relatively uniform (Larsell, 1970) and is therefore ideal for the comparison of homologous neural circuits across species (Smaers, 2014a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the uniform anatomy of the cerebellum, supported by citations.

claim: The lateral extension of the cerebellum to form distinct hemispheres arose early in mammalian evolution.
source: Second, the lateral extension of the cerebellum to form distinct hemispheres arose early in mammalian evolution (Figure 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1 showing cerebellar anatomy across species.

claim: The lateral cerebellum has been hypothesized to be involved in the generation of domain-general higher-order models of mental activity through its connectional integration with heteromodal association areas in the cerebrum.
source: Third, through its connectional integration with heteromodal association areas in the cerebrum, the lateral cerebellum has been hypothesized to be involved in the generation of domain-general higher-order models of mental activity.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on connectional anatomy.

claim: The cerebellum imposes a type of cognitive control over information processing that consists of automating sequences of thoughts and actions.
source: A central working hypothesis in this context is that the cerebellum imposes a type of cognitive control over information processing that consists of automating sequences of thoughts and actions (Schmahmann, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a working hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Cerebellar-type cognitive control may underpin many aspects associated with 'intelligent' behavior, such as working memory, executive function, and the development of behavioral learning models.
source: This cerebellar-type cognitive control may underpin many aspects associated with 'intelligent' behavior, such as working memory, executive function, and the development of behavioral learning models (Strick et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility supported by a citation.

claim: The strong connectional and functional integration between the lateral cerebellar hemisphere and the cerebrum is evident in developmental modularity.
source: Finally, the strong connectional and functional integration between the lateral cerebellar hemisphere and the cerebrum is also evident in developmental modularity.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about developmental modularity.

claim: The medial cerebellum develops early, while the lateral cerebellum develops later in tandem with cerebral association areas.
source: Whereas the medial cerebellum develops early, the lateral cerebellum develops later in tandem with cerebral association areas (Tiemeier et al., 2010; Altman and Bayer, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Barn owls lack lateral cerebellar hemispheres.
source: Note the absence of lateral cerebellar hemispheres in the barn owl.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cerebellar volume is a nearly linear function of its number of neurons.
source: Volumetric measurements of cerebellar partitions were used because cerebellar volume is a nearly linear function of its number of neurons (Herculano-Houzel, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Phylogenetic scaling of lateral to medial cerebellar volume indicates a positive scaling trend with F = 294.6, p<0.001, λ = 0.945.
source: Phylogenetic scaling of lateral to medial cerebellar volume indicates a positive scaling trend (F = 294.6, p<0.001, λ = 0.945)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: The slope of lateral to medial cerebellar volume scaling is higher than unity with a 95% confidence interval of 1.167:1.478.
source: with a slope that is higher than unity (95% confidence interval: 1.167:1.478) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ratio of observed to predicted lateral to medial cerebellar values ranges from 2.3 to 4.4 in apes, cetaceans and pinnipeds.
source: The ratio of the observed to the predicted values range from 2.3 to 4.4 in apes, cetaceans and pinnipeds
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The ratio of observed to predicted lateral to medial cerebellar values ranges from 0.6 to 0.7 in feliformes.
source: from 0.6 to 0.7 in feliformes
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The ratio of observed to predicted lateral to medial cerebellar values ranges from 0.2 to 0.3 in artiodactyls.
source: and from 0.2 to 0.3 in artiodactyls.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization is a significant predictor of domain-general cognition in primates (F = 15.670, p=0.001).
source: Phylogenetic regression analysis also demonstrated that lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization is a significant predictor of domain-general cognition in primates (F = 15.670, p=0.001, Figure 2)
evidence: This is a statistical result from phylogenetic regression analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Five shifts in mean value of lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization occurred with posterior probability >0.8.
source: This analysis indicates five shifts in mean value with a posterior probability ('PP')>0.8.
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian reversible-jump OU analysis.

claim: Regime shifts in lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization occurred at the root branches of the apes, the cetartiodactyls, the cetaceans, the pinnipeds, and the feliformes.
source: These regime shifts occurred at the root branches of the apes, the cetartiodactyls, the cetaceans (note that our sample includes toothed whales only), the pinnipeds, and the feliformes (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian reversible-jump OU analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio of the estimated pattern of lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization is 52.34.
source: The signal-to-noise ratio of this estimated pattern is 52.34, demonstrating that the analysis has high effect size and high power.
evidence: This is a statistical measure of the reliability of the analysis.

claim: The regime shifts in lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization represent significant differences in the intercept of lateral to medial cerebellar scaling (grade shifts).
source: Phylogenetic analysis of covariance (Smaers and Rohlf, 2016) indicates that these shifts represent significant differences in the intercept of lateral to medial cerebellar scaling (i.e. grade shifts; Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic ANCOVA shown in Table 1.

claim: Apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds are not significantly different from each other in lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization.
source: Specifically, apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds are not significantly different from each other, but each (and as a group) are significantly different from others.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic ANCOVA.

claim: Apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds are significantly different from other mammals in lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization.
source: Specifically, apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds are not significantly different from each other, but each (and as a group) are significantly different from others.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic ANCOVA.

claim: Feliformes and artiodactyls are not significantly different from each other in lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization.
source: Furthermore, feliformes and artiodactyls are not significantly different from each other, but each (and as a group) are significantly different from others.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic ANCOVA.

claim: Feliformes and artiodactyls are significantly different from other mammals in lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization.
source: Furthermore, feliformes and artiodactyls are not significantly different from each other, but each (and as a group) are significantly different from others.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic ANCOVA.

claim: The six regimes identified by OU modelling constitute three significantly different grades of lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization.
source: These results demonstrate that the six regimes identified by OU modelling constitute three significantly different grades (in order of magnitude of relative lateral to medial cerebellar size): apes, toothed whales, and pinnipeds (grade 1); rest of the sample (grade 2); artiodactyls and feliformes (grade 3).
evidence: This is a synthesis of the phylogenetic ANCOVA results.

claim: The equality of slopes assumption of analysis of covariance is upheld for the three grades of lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization.
source: The equality of slopes assumption of analysis of covariance is upheld (grade 1 versus grade 2: F = 0.009, p=0.925; grade 1 versus grade 3: F = 0.088, p=0.771; grade 2 versus grade 3: F = 0.836, p=0.367).
evidence: This is a statistical validation of the ANCOVA assumptions.

claim: No regime shifts in relative cerebellum size were found with posterior probability >0.8.
source: These analyses revealed no regime shifts indicating PP >0.8
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian reversible-jump OU analysis for relative cerebellum size.

claim: A single regime shift in relative cerebellum size was found with PP >0.5 at the ancestral lineage of the zebu (PP = 0.76).
source: and only a single regime shift with PP >0.5 (the ancestral lineage of the zebu (Bos taurus indicus): PP = 0.76).
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian reversible-jump OU analysis for relative cerebellum size.

claim: Two regime shifts in relative cerebellum size had 0.2 < PP < 0.5: the root of musteline carnivorans (0.38), and cercopithecine primates (0.29).
source: Two other regimes shifts had 0.2 < PP < 0.5: the root of musteline carnivorans (0.38), and cercopithecine primates (0.29) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian reversible-jump OU analysis for relative cerebellum size.

claim: For relative cerebellar size, observed/predicted values range from 1.2 to 1.6 for musteline carnivorans.
source: For relative cerebellar size observed/predicted values ranges from 1.2 to 1.6 for musteline carnivorans
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: For relative cerebellar size, observed/predicted values range from 0.7 to 0.9 for cercopithecine primates.
source: from 0.7 to 0.9 for cercopithecine primates
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: For relative cerebellar size, the observed/predicted value is 0.5 for the zebu.
source: and 0.5 for the zebu.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Relative cerebellum size is not a significant predictor of domain-general cognition in primates (F = 2.122, p=0.163).
source: Phylogenetic regression analysis demonstrated that relative cerebellum size is not a significant predictor of domain-general cognition in primates (lateral-medial: F = 2.122, p=0.163).
evidence: This is a statistical result from phylogenetic regression analysis.

claim: Rates of evolution were found to be significantly different between lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization and relative cerebellum size (p=0.002) at a ratio of 2.9.
source: Rates were found to be significantly different (p=0.002) at a ratio of 2.9 (lateral to medial cerebellum σ2 = 0.00753, relative cerebellum size σ2 = 0.00261).
evidence: This is a result from Q-mode rate analysis.

claim: Apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds are not significantly different in relative medial cerebellum size.
source: Results indicate that apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds are not significantly different in relative medial cerebellum size (apes versus toothed whales and pinnipeds: F = 1.06, p=0.31; toothed whales versus apes and pinnipeds: F = 1.11, p=0.30; pinnipeds versus apes and toothed whales: F = 0.07, p=0.79).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic ANCOVA.

claim: Analysis of lateral cerebellum size versus rest of brain size yields similar results as the lateral to medial comparison in that apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds are not significantly different from each other, but are different from other mammals.
source: Furthermore, analysis of lateral cerebellum size versus rest of brain size yields similar results as the lateral to medial comparison in that apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds are not significantly different from each other, but are different from other mammals (apes versus toothed whales and pinnipeds: F < 0.01, p=0.96; toothed whales versus apes and pinnipeds: F = 1.13, p=0.29; pinnipeds versus apes and toothed whales: F = 0.56, p=0.45; apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds versus others (holding constant artiodactyls and feliforms): F = 5.06, p=0.01).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic ANCOVA.

claim: The convergent lateral to medial reorganization among apes, toothed whales and pinnipeds is not due to a differential effect on medial and/or lateral cerebellum size, but rather to a similarly convergent pattern of lateral to medial reorganization.
source: These results confirm that the convergent lateral to medial reorganization among these clades is not due to a differential effect on medial and/or lateral cerebellum size, but rather, that it is due to a similarly convergent pattern of lateral to medial reorganization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phylogenetic ANCOVA results.

claim: Results demonstrate a combination of parallel and convergent evolutionary events in mammals leading to relative lateral cerebellar expansion.
source: Results demonstrate a combination of parallel and convergent evolutionary events in mammals leading to relative lateral cerebellar expansion.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: The evolutionary pattern of lateral cerebellar expansion encompasses distantly related lineages - apes, toothed whales, and pinnipeds.
source: This evolutionary pattern encompasses distantly related lineages - apes, toothed whales, and pinnipeds.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: The congruence between apes and pinnipeds demonstrates parallel evolution as they derive from a similar ancestral condition.
source: The congruence between apes and pinnipeds demonstrates parallel evolution as they derive from a similar ancestral condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the evolutionary pattern based on phylogenetic relationships.

claim: The congruence with toothed whales demonstrates convergence as they derive from a different ancestral condition (evident in the artiodactyls grade with smaller relative lateral cerebellar size).
source: The congruence with toothed whales demonstrates convergence as they derive from a different ancestral condition (evident in the artiodactyls grade with smaller relative lateral cerebellar size).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the evolutionary pattern based on phylogenetic relationships.

claim: The cerebellum has been hypothesized to be involved in the domain-general automation of associative learning abilities.
source: The cerebellum has been hypothesized to be involved in the domain-general automation of associative learning abilities (Schmahmann, 1997)
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: The cerebellum may be a target of evolution leading to the emergence of 'intelligent' behaviors.
source: The cerebellum has been hypothesized to be involved in the domain-general automation of associative learning abilities (Schmahmann, 1997) and, according to the results of the present analyses, may be a target of evolution leading to the emergence of 'intelligent' behaviors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: The contribution of the cerebellum's role to cognition has been hypothesized to lie in the extrapolation of error-based motor learning processes to domains beyond motor control such as social cognition.
source: Specifically, the contribution of the cerebellum's role to cognition has been hypothesized to lie in the extrapolation of error-based motor learning processes to domains beyond motor control such as social cognition (Sokolov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: According to theoretical models of cerebellar function, the cerebellum receives a copy of the motor command and generates a representation ('internal model') of the expected consequences of that command.
source: According to theoretical models of cerebellar function, the cerebellum receives a copy of the motor command and generates a representation ('internal model') of the expected consequences of that command (Sokolov et al., 2017; Ito, 2008; Moberget and Ivry, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical model supported by citations.

claim: Sensory prediction ('forward model') allows for predictive control of motor actions which results in smooth and automated execution.
source: Such sensory prediction ('forward model') allows for predictive control of motor actions which results in smooth and automated execution (Koziol et al., 20132014).
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism supported by a citation.

claim: In humans, evidence has been found that the cerebellar process of sensory prediction, in addition to being active in relation to motor actions, may also be active in semantic processing.
source: In humans, evidence has been found that this process, in addition to being active in relation to motor actions, may also be active in semantic processing (Moberget et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In humans, evidence has been found that the cerebellar process of sensory prediction may be active in social cognition.
source: In humans, evidence has been found that this process, in addition to being active in relation to motor actions, may also be active in semantic processing (Moberget et al., 2014), and social cognition (Van Overwalle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The measure of cognitive ability in primates used in this study quantifies the performance of animals on nine tasks that are independent of perceptual bias and contextual confounds.
source: This measure of cognitive ability in primates quantifies the performance of animals on nine tasks that are independent of perceptual bias and contextual confounds (Deaner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral measure used, supported by a citation.

claim: The positive correlation between lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization and domain-general cognition provides indirect support for the hypothesis that the cerebellum is involved in cognition.
source: This positive correlation provides indirect support for the hypothesis that the cerebellum is involved in cognition
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation result.

claim: The association between lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization and cognition may have deep evolutionary roots.
source: This positive correlation provides indirect support for the hypothesis that the cerebellum is involved in cognition, and further suggests that this association may have deep evolutionary roots.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of the correlation.

claim: Primates are the only order for which a standardized measure of higher cognitive capacity is available that matches available cerebellar data.
source: Unfortunately, Primates are the only order for which a standardized measure of higher cognitive capacity is available that matches available cerebellar data.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the available data.

claim: Vocal production learning (VPL) is defined as the ability to modify existing vocalizations and to imitate novel sounds not belonging to the innate repertoire.
source: VPL is defined as the ability to modify existing vocalizations and to imitate novel sounds not belonging to the innate repertoire (Janik and Slater, 2000).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: VPL aligns with 'cerebellar-type' error-based learning in that it results in smooth and automated execution after combining individual motor actions into a more complex automated model.
source: VPL aligns with 'cerebellar-type' error-based learning in that it results in smooth and automated execution after combining individual motor actions into a more complex automated model.
evidence: This is a theoretical connection made by the authors.

claim: In humans, the link between cerebellum and vocal learning is supported by an association between lateral cerebellar activation patterns and semantic processing.
source: In humans, the link between cerebellum and vocal learning is supported by an association between lateral cerebellar activation patterns and semantic processing (Moberget et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In mammals, only a few species are known to be capable of VPL: humans, bats, elephants, seals, dolphins, and toothed whales.
source: In mammals, only a few species are known to be capable of VPL: humans, bats (Vernes, 2017), elephants (Stoeger et al., 2012), seals (Ralls et al., 1985; Ravignani et al., 2016), dolphins (Reiss and McCowan, 1993), and toothed whales (Foote et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Apart from bats, all mammalian species capable of VPL have increased lateral cerebella.
source: Apart from bats (not included in our sample due to a lack of available data on cerebellar hemispheres), our analyses indicate that all these species have increased lateral cerebella
evidence: This is a result from the analyses.

claim: Elephants indicate a pronounced trend of lateral cerebellar expansion, though this trend is not significant in the sample.
source: (though note that although our analysis demonstrates that elephants indicate a pronounced trend of lateral cerebellar expansion, this trend is not significant in our sample).
evidence: This is a result from the analyses with a caveat about statistical significance.

claim: The congruence between results on multiple independent evolutionary expansion events of the mammalian lateral cerebellum and the occurrence of the capacity for VPL is further support of an evolutionary association between changes in cerebellar processing and cognition.
source: The congruence between our results on multiple independent evolutionary expansion events of the mammalian lateral cerebellum and the occurrence of the capacity for VPL is further support of an evolutionary association between changes in cerebellar processing and cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the cerebellar expansion results with VPL data.

claim: A potential link between cognitive specializations and convergent lateral cerebellar expansion suggests that repeated selection on a common neural substrate has, at least partly, characterized mammalian brain evolution in relation to cognition.
source: A potential link between such cognitive specializations and convergent lateral cerebellar expansion suggests that repeated selection on a common neural substrate has, at least partly, characterized mammalian brain evolution in relation to cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: The occurrence of convergent lateral cerebellar expansion does not exclude the concomitant occurrence of lineage-specific adaptive specializations in other parts of the brain, such as the neocortex.
source: This, however, does not exclude the concomitant occurrence of lineage-specific adaptive specializations in other parts of the brain, such as the neocortex.
evidence: This is a caveat to the interpretation.

claim: Different orders of mammals may have neocortices that are organized in fundamentally different ways.
source: The available information suggests that different orders of mammals may have neocortices that are organized in fundamentally different ways.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation from the literature.

claim: Primates have evolved a suite of novel fronto-parietal cortical areas that form a network that is functionally, hodologically, and developmentally linked.
source: Primates, for example, have evolved a suite of novel fronto-parietal cortical areas that form a network that is functionally, hodologically, and developmentally linked.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about primate brain organization.

claim: The primate-specific fronto-parietal network is not observed in other mammals.
source: Crucially, this primate-specific network is not observed in other mammals (Preuss, 2007; Preuss, 1995; Preuss and Goldman-Rakic, 1991a; Preuss and Goldman-Rakic, 1991b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Order-specific specializations lend support to the hypothesis that species differences in intelligence can, at least partly, be understood as an interaction between aggregates of domain-specific abilities, together with changes in domain-general processing.
source: Such order-specific specializations lend support to the hypothesis that species differences in intelligence can, at least partly, be understood as an interaction between aggregates of domain-specific abilities, together with changes in domain-general processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting order-specific specializations with theories of intelligence.

claim: Cerebellar partitions that are hypothesized to underpin domain-general associative learning abilities have repeatedly been subject to directional selection.
source: Indeed, our current results demonstrate that those cerebellar partitions that are hypothesized to underpin domain-general associative learning abilities have repeatedly been subject to directional selection
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: Modification of common neural systems may contribute significantly to the evolution of animal intelligence.
source: suggesting that modification of common neural systems may contribute significantly to the evolution of animal intelligence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: The nature of cerebellar microstructural circuit anatomy is fairly uniform across mammals.
source: The nature of cerebellar microstructural circuit anatomy (fairly uniform across mammals)
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the cerebellum.

claim: The hypothesized function of the cerebellum is to automate and streamline cerebral information processing.
source: and hypothesized function (to automate and streamline cerebral information processing)
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis about cerebellar function.

claim: The domain-general features of the cerebellum have been repeatedly subject to selection, irrespective of the precise organization of the cerebral cortex in different orders.
source: lends support to our conclusion that its domain-general features have been repeatedly subject to selection, irrespective of the precise organization of the cerebral cortex in different orders.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results and the nature of cerebellar anatomy.

claim: Across orders, the evolution of the mammalian brain may be characterized by something new (cerebral specializations) and something borrowed (cerebellar convergences).
source: Across orders, the evolution of the mammalian brain may hereby be characterized by something new (cerebral specializations) and something borrowed (cerebellar convergences).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the evolutionary pattern.

claim: In primates, the lateral cerebellum's role in cognitive processing is tightly linked to higher-order visual and somatosensory cortical association areas.
source: In primates, the lateral cerebellum's role in cognitive processing is tightly linked to higher-order visual and somatosensory cortical association areas (Preuss, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Primates evolved specializations for visual grasping and reaching that involved extensive integration of visual, motor, and somatosensory processing.
source: Primates evolved specializations for visual grasping and reaching that involved extensive integration of visual, motor, and somatosensory processing (Wise et al., 1997; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cortical association areas involved in visual grasping and reaching specializations are connected to lateral cerebellar lobules.
source: Accordingly, cortical association areas involved in these specializations are connected to lateral cerebellar lobules (O'Reilly et al., 2010; Ramnani et al., 2006; Glickstein et al., 2011; Sokolov et al., 2014; Schmahmann and Pandya, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The nature of cortico-cerebellar hodology in toothed whales and pinnipeds is less well described than in primates.
source: The nature of cortico-cerebellar hodology in toothed whales and pinnipeds is, however, less well described.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current knowledge.

claim: Previous research provides indirect evidence for the expansion of cortical association areas in toothed whales and pinnipeds.
source: Although previous research provides indirect evidence for the expansion of cortical association areas in these groups (van Kann et al., 2017; Hof and Van Der Gucht, 2007; Hof et al., 2005; Turner et al., 2017; Sawyer et al., 2016), more research is needed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research, with a caveat that more research is needed.

claim: Cortical information processing in toothed whales is geared more towards auditory processing (echolocation).
source: It is clear, however, that cortical information processing in toothed whales is geared more towards auditory processing (echolocation)
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about toothed whale brain organization.

claim: In pinnipeds, as in terrestrial carnivorans and primates, cortical information processing is geared more towards vision.
source: while in pinnipeds, as in terrestrial carnivorans and primates, it is geared more towards vision.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about pinniped brain organization.

claim: Pinnipeds evolved exceptional somatosensory and visual sensitivity rather than echolocation to navigate a poorly visible aquatic niche.
source: Rather than evolving echolocation to navigate a poorly visible aquatic niche, pinnipeds evolved exceptional somatosensory and visual sensitivity (Hanke et al., 2009; Scholtyssek et al., 2008; Dehnhardt et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The differences between toothed whales (auditory specializations for echolocation) and primates and pinnipeds (visual and somatosensory specializations) accord with preliminary observations that the enlargement of the lateral cerebellum in toothed whales may be due to the expansion of different lobules within the hemisphere, as compared with apes and pinnipeds.
source: The differences between toothed whales (auditory specializations for echolocation) and primates and pinnipeds (visual and somatosensory specializations) accord with preliminary observations that the enlargement of the lateral cerebellum in toothed whales may be due to the expansion of different lobules within the hemisphere, as compared with apes and pinnipeds.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting sensory specializations with cerebellar anatomy.

claim: Hemispheric expansion in apes is most likely due to the enlargement of lobule HVII.
source: Whereas hemispheric expansion in apes is most likely due to the enlargement of lobule HVII (Balsters et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Lobule HVII connects closely to cortical association areas such as temporal, parietal and prefrontal cortex, which are involved in visually-guided actions.
source: (which connects closely to cortical association areas such as temporal, parietal and prefrontal cortex, which are involved in visually-guided actions)
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the connectivity of lobule HVII.

claim: Hemispheric expansion in toothed whales may be due to enlargement of lobule HIX.
source: hemispheric expansion in toothed whales may be due to enlargement of lobule HIX (Jansen and Jansen, 1969)
evidence: This is stated as a possibility supported by a citation.

claim: Lobule HIX in toothed whales is possibly more closely connected to auditory processing.
source: (possibly more closely connected to auditory processing).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation.

claim: Hemispheric expansion in pinnipeds is speculated to be due to lobule HVII, given that visual and somatosensory specializations are prominent in both primates and pinnipeds.
source: Given that visual and somatosensory specializations are prominent in both primates and pinnipeds, we speculate that hemispheric expansion in pinnipeds is also due to lobule HVII.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on sensory specializations.

claim: Visually dominant birds such as crows, parrots, and woodpeckers have enlarged visually projecting lobules VI–IX (in the medial cerebellum).
source: Similarly, visually dominant birds such as crows, parrots, and woodpeckers have enlarged visually projecting lobules VI–IX (in the medial cerebellum; birds do not have lateral extensions of the cerebellum, see Figure 1), likely related to their repertoire of visually guided goal-directed beak behavior (Sultan, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Birds do not have lateral extensions of the cerebellum.
source: birds do not have lateral extensions of the cerebellum, see Figure 1
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The lower than expected relative lateral cerebellar size in artiodactyls and felines should be confirmed with increased sampling.
source: The lower than expected relative lateral cerebellar size in artiodactyls and felines should be confirmed with increased sampling.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the results.

claim: The artiodactyls and felines may better reflect an early ancestral condition of lateral cerebellar size.
source: Considering that the lateral expansion of cerebellar lobules is a feature that first arose in early mammals, the artiodactyls and felines may, in fact, better reflect an early ancestral condition.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility.

claim: If artiodactyls and felines reflect an early ancestral condition, the extent of the convergent and parallel expansion in apes, toothed whales, and pinnipeds would be an underestimation of the true trend.
source: In this scenario, the extent of the convergent and parallel expansion in apes, toothed whales, and pinnipeds observed here would be an underestimation of the true trend.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the previous speculation.

claim: Previous studies on cerebellar evolution have mainly considered the cerebellum as a whole.
source: Previous studies on cerebellar evolution have mainly considered the cerebellum as a whole.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of previous research.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that the cerebellum underwent rapid size increase (relative to the cerebral cortex considered as a whole) in apes.
source: These studies have suggested that the cerebellum underwent rapid size increase (relative to the cerebral cortex considered as a whole) in apes (Barton and Venditti, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that the elephant has the largest relative cerebellum size of all mammals.
source: and that the elephant has the largest relative cerebellum size of all mammals (Maseko et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: After accounting for scaling differences with the rest of brain size, relative cerebellum size shows a grade shift in apes (pANCOVA, F = 5.432, p=0.024).
source: After accounting for scaling differences with the rest of brain size, our results confirm that relative cerebellum size shows a grade shift in apes (pANCOVA, F = 5.432, p=0.024)
evidence: This is a statistical result from phylogenetic ANCOVA.

claim: There is no evidence to support the conclusion that relative cerebellar size is significantly expanded in elephants compared to other mammals (pANCOVA, F = 2.426, p=0.126).
source: but we found no evidence to support the conclusion that relative cerebellar size is significantly expanded in elephants compared to other mammals (pANCOVA, F = 2.426, p=0.126).
evidence: This is a statistical result from phylogenetic ANCOVA.

claim: Bayesian reversible-jump estimation of multi-peak OU models indicates that the patterns of grade shifts in apes and elephants are not the most dominant in characterizing the macroevolutionary landscape of relative cerebellum size.
source: However, Bayesian reversible-jump estimation of multi-peak OU models indicates that neither of these patterns are the most dominant in characterizing the macroevolutionary landscape of relative cerebellum size.
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian OU modeling.

claim: The macroevolutionary landscape of relative cerebellar size is primarily characterized by a significant decrease in the zebu (observed/allometrically predicted value = 0.52) and cercopithecine primates (observed/allometrically predicted value = 0.85), and an increase in the musteline carnivorans (observed/allometrically predicted value = 1.44).
source: Rather, the macroevolutionary landscape of relative cerebellar size is primarily characterized by a significant decrease in the zebu (observed/allometrically predicted value = 0.52) and cercopithecine primates (observed/allometrically predicted value = 0.85), and an increase in the musteline carnivorans (observed/allometrically predicted value = 1.44) (SI1, SI5).
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian OU modeling.

claim: A comparison of the rate of evolution of lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization against relative cerebellum size shows a significantly higher rate for lateral-medial reorganization.
source: Furthermore, a comparison of the rate of evolution of lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization against relative cerebellum size shows a significantly higher rate for lateral-medial reorganization (Figure 4)
evidence: This is a result from rate analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The main result of selective pressure in mammalian cerebellar evolution has led to modular changes within the cerebellum (likely related to reciprocal loops of information processing with particular cerebral networks), rather than global changes in cerebellum size relative to overall brain size or overall cerebral cortex size.
source: suggesting that the main result of selective pressure in mammalian cerebellar evolution has led to modular changes within the cerebellum (likely related to reciprocal loops of information processing with particular cerebral networks), rather than global changes in cerebellum size relative to overall brain size or overall cerebral cortex (or 'neocortex') size.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rate comparison results.

claim: The results accord with the cerebellum's functional, connectional, and developmental modularity.
source: These results also accord with the cerebellum's functional, connectional, and developmental modularity.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the results with known cerebellar properties.

claim: Some argue that volumetric reorganization occurs predominantly in a 'mosaic' fashion as a result of behavioral selective pressures which is largely unconstrained by developmental patterning.
source: Some argue that volumetric reorganization occurs predominantly in a 'mosaic' fashion as a result of behavioral selective pressures which is largely unconstrained by developmental patterning (Barton, 2006; Barton and Harvey, 2000; Barton, 2001).
evidence: This is a characterization of one view in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Others argue that the sequence of developmental events plays a more significant role in shaping brain reorganization such that earlier developing structures are more likely to be evolutionarily conservative than later developing structures.
source: Others argue that the sequence of developmental events plays a more significant role in shaping brain reorganization such that earlier developing structures are more likely to be evolutionarily conservative than later developing structures (Finlay et al., 2001; Finlay and Darlington, 1995).
evidence: This is a characterization of another view in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Cerebellar reorganization occurs in alignment with developmental predictions, with the later developing partition (the lateral cerebellum) showing a higher rate of evolution and characterized by a more complex evolutionary scenario than the earlier developing partition (the medial cerebellum).
source: Our results indicate that cerebellar reorganization occurs in alignment with developmental predictions, with the later developing partition (i.c. the lateral cerebellum) showing a higher rate of evolution and characterized by a more complex evolutionary scenario than the earlier developing partition (i.c. the medial cerebellum) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results shown in the figures.

claim: Mammalian cerebellar reorganization is more consistent with modular change (reorganization predicated on developmental patterning), than it is with mosaic change (reorganization largely unconstrained by developmental patterning).
source: Mammalian cerebellar reorganization is therefore more consistent with modular change (i.e. reorganization predicated on developmental patterning), than it is with mosaic change (i.e. reorganization largely unconstrained by developmental patterning).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: In primates, lateral cerebellar evolution appears to be particularly linked with those cerebral association areas that are part of the primate-specific cerebro-cerebellar network.
source: In primates, lateral cerebellar evolution appears to be particularly linked with those cerebral association areas that are part of the primate-specific cerebro-cerebellar network (Smaers, 2014a; Balsters et al., 2010; Smaers et al., 2013; Smaers et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A similar grade shift in great apes and humans is observed in the primate-specific cerebro-cerebellar network.
source: where a similar grade shift in great apes and humans is observed (Smaers et al., 2017; Passingham and Smaers, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The occurrence of significant changes in cerebellar structural reorganization in the mammalian macroevolutionary landscape, combined with the higher rate of evolution for changes in lateral-medial cerebellar organization over changes in relative cerebellar size, draws attention to a new avenue of adaptive brain evolution.
source: The occurrence of significant changes in cerebellar structural reorganization in the mammalian macroevolutionary landscape (Figure 3), combined with the higher rate of evolution for changes in lateral-medial cerebellar organization over changes in relative cerebellar size (Figure 4) draws attention to a new avenue of adaptive brain evolution.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined results.

claim: Across mammals, the total number of cerebellar neurons (excluding Purkinje neurons) correlates significantly with the number of cerebral neurons.
source: Across mammals, the total number of cerebellar neurons (excluding Purkinje neurons) correlates significantly with the number of cerebral neurons, leading to the suggestion that coordinated processing networks with the neocortex constrain cerebellar evolution(Herculano-Houzel, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Analyses of cerebellar evolution have rarely accounted for modular reorganization within gross anatomical structures independently of overall size.
source: To date, however, such analyses have rarely accounted for modular reorganization within gross anatomical structures (such as the cerebellum and the neocortex) independently of overall size (but see Balsters et al. (2010)).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous research.

claim: The significant grade shifts in cerebellar reorganization show that not all scaled up cerebella are anatomically homologous.
source: The significant grade shifts in cerebellar reorganization observed here show that not all scaled up cerebella are anatomically homologous.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the grade shift results.

claim: Apes, toothed whales, and pinnipeds have lateral cerebellar hemispheres that are 2.3 to 4.4 times larger than predicted relative to the medial cerebellum.
source: A comparison of observed to allometrically predicted values indicate that apes, toothed whales, and pinnipeds have lateral cerebellar hemispheres that are 2.3 to 4.4 times larger than predicted relative to the medial cerebellum
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Artiodactyls have lateral cerebella that are 3.3 to 4.4 times smaller than predicted relative to the medial cerebellum.
source: while artiodactyls have lateral cerebella that are 3.3 to 4.4 times smaller than predicted.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Given near isometric scaling of number of neurons and mass in the cerebellum, the relative number of neurons dedicated to automating either higher cerebral association processing (lateral cerebellum), or basic motor skills and proprioception (medial cerebellum) is similarly unevenly distributed in apes, toothed whales, and pinnipeds versus artiodactyls.
source: Given near isometric scaling of number of neurons and mass in the cerebellum, this implies that the relative number of neurons dedicated to automating either higher cerebral association processing (lateral cerebellum), or basic motor skills and proprioception (medial cerebellum) is similarly unevenly distributed in apes, toothed whales, and pinnipeds versus artiodactyls.
evidence: This is an inference based on the scaling relationship and the observed differences.

claim: The artiodactyls in the sample have similarly sized brains than apes and pinnipeds.
source: Moreover, the artiodactyls in our sample have similarly sized brains than apes and pinnipeds, further demonstrating the importance of modular reorganization patterns that are independent of brain size.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Cerebellar cells (mostly granule cells) are more densely packed in eulipotyphlans, primates, and elephants, compared to other mammals investigated.
source: For instance, cerebellar cells (mostly granule cells) are more densely packed in eulipotyphlans, primates, and elephants, compared to other mammals investigated (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Remarkable differences in the ratio of granule cells to Purkinje neurons have been reported, with the greatest proportions of granule cells per Purkinje neuron found in primates, toothed whales, and elephants.
source: And remarkable differences in the ratio of granule cells to Purkinje neurons have been reported, with the greatest proportions of granule cells per Purkinje neuron found in primates, toothed whales, and elephants (Lange, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Golgi impregnation studies have demonstrated that cerebellar neuron morphologies vary across mammals, showing strikingly extensive dendritic branching of Lugaro cells in elephants.
source: Additionally, Golgi impregnation studies have demonstrated that cerebellar neuron morphologies vary across mammals, showing strikingly extensive dendritic branching of Lugaro cells in elephants (Jacobs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The functional impact of species differences in cerebellar microstructure is yet to be fully understood.
source: The functional impact of such species differences in microstructure is yet to be fully understood, but should be considered alongside volumetric reorganization in a comprehensive model of cerebellar evolution.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current knowledge.

claim: A tendency for distantly related mammalian species to converge on lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization plays an important role in explaining cerebellar macroevolution.
source: We conclude that a tendency for distantly related mammalian species to converge on lateral-medial cerebellar reorganization plays an important role in explaining cerebellar macroevolution.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Considering the lateral cerebellum's hypothesized role in automating higher-order cortical association information processing, the macroevolutionary pattern suggests a tendency for distantly related species to independently acquire 'cerebellar-like' associative-learning abilities.
source: Considering the lateral cerebellum's hypothesized role in automating higher-order cortical association information processing, this macroevolutionary pattern suggests a tendency for distantly related species to independently acquire 'cerebellar-like' associative-learning abilities.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the macroevolutionary pattern.

claim: Cerebellar reorganization is a target for broad comparative investigations of neurobiological diversification because it is more reflective of modularity and interconnectivity than overall brain size.
source: We propose cerebellar reorganization as a target for broad comparative investigations of neurobiological diversification because it is more reflective of modularity and interconnectivity than overall brain size
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings.

claim: Cerebellar reorganization more validly represents homologous functional and neural circuitry than the more traditional focus on overall neocortex.
source: and more validly represents homologous functional and neural circuitry than the more traditional focus on overall neocortex.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings.

claim: Brain data were taken from MacLeod et al. (2003), Smaers et al. (2011), and Maseko et al. (2012).
source: Brain data were taken from MacLeod et al. (2003), Smaers et al. (2011), and Maseko et al. (2012).
evidence: This describes the data sources.

claim: Behavioral data were taken from Deaner et al. (2006).
source: Behavioral data were taken from Deaner et al. (2006).
evidence: This describes the data sources.

claim: The phylogeny was adjusted from Faurby and Svenning (2015), who used a novel heuristic-hierarchical Bayesian approach for estimating a species-rich phylogeny of mammals.
source: The phylogeny was adjusted from Faurby and Svenning (2015), who used a novel heuristic-hierarchical Bayesian approach for estimating a species-rich (>4100 species) phylogeny of mammals.
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic methods.

claim: The focus of the study lies on the comparison between the lateral and medial cerebellum.
source: The focus of our study lies on the comparison between the lateral and medial cerebellum.
evidence: This describes the methodological focus.

claim: The measure of lateral to medial cerebellum quantifies changes within the cerebellum between its two major constituent partitions that are functionally, connectionally, and developmentally distinct.
source: This measure quantifies changes within the cerebellum between its two major constituent partitions that are functionally, connectionally, and developmentally distinct.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the measure used.

claim: The medial (vermis and paravermis) cerebellum is involved in basic motor control, proprioception and autonomic functions.
source: Whereas the medial (vermis and paravermis) cerebellum is involved in basic motor control, proprioception and autonomic functions
evidence: This is stated as a fact about cerebellar function.

claim: The lateral hemispheres are the site of integration for multiple streams of cerebral information processing.
source: the lateral hemispheres are the site of integration for multiple streams of cerebral information processing (Glickstein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The measure of overall cerebellar size relative to the size of the rest of the brain overlooks modularity within the cerebellum.
source: Although this latter measure is the most commonly used in previous research, it overlooks modularity within the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a critique of an alternative measure.

claim: The measure of overall cerebellar size relative to the rest of the brain does not account for the fact that the cerebellum is highly interconnected with much of the rest of the brain.
source: Moreover, this measure also does not account for the fact that the cerebellum is highly interconnected with much of the rest of the brain.
evidence: This is a critique of an alternative measure.

claim: A comparison of cerebellum against the rest of the brain performs a statistical control for much of what is neurobiologically relevant.
source: A comparison against the rest of the brain thus performs a statistical control for much of what is neurobiologically relevant.
evidence: This is a critique of an alternative measure.

claim: The study primarily focuses on the measure of lateral to medial cerebellum because it represents the cerebellum's modular organization and is therefore more relevant to understanding the underpinnings of neural information processing.
source: We primarily focus on the measure of lateral to medial cerebellum because it represents the cerebellum's modular organization and is therefore more relevant to understanding the underpinnings of neural information processing (Passingham and Smaers, 2014).
evidence: This is the rationale for the methodological choice, supported by a citation.
